16: # Cross-AI Orchestration Patterns: Calling AI + Codex CLI
17: 
18: Proven patterns for orchestrating Codex CLI from any AI assistant session.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Core Principle
25: 
26: The calling AI acts as the orchestrator (planner, validator, integrator) while Codex CLI executes targeted tasks. The value comes from combining different model perspectives and leveraging Codex's sandbox-controlled execution, not from redundant work.
27: 
28: ### Purpose
29: 
30: Each pattern documented here includes the rationale, implementation template, and practical considerations for combining the calling AI with Codex CLI effectively.
31: 
32: ### When to Use
33: 
34: - You need a second AI perspective on generated code, architecture, or security
35: - Codex's strengths (sandbox isolation, `xhigh` reasoning, web search via `--search`) complement the calling AI's strengths
36: - You want to run parallel AI tasks while the calling AI continues working
37: - Complex workflows benefit from structured, multi-stage generation and validation
38: - You need controlled file modification with sandbox-enforced safety boundaries
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## 2. GENERATE-REVIEW-FIX CYCLE
43: 
44: **The most reliable cross-AI pattern.** One AI generates, the other reviews, then the original fixes.
45: 
46: ### Flow
47: 
48: ```
49: Calling AI (plan) --> Codex CLI (generate) --> Calling AI (review) --> Codex CLI (fix)
50: ```
51: 
52: ### Implementation
53: 
54: ```bash
55: # Step 1: Codex generates the code
56: codex exec \
57:   "Create a rate limiter middleware for Express with sliding window algorithm. Output only the code, no explanation." \
58:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/rate-limiter.ts
59: 
60: # Step 2: Calling AI reviews (done within the calling AI session)
61: # Read /tmp/rate-limiter.ts, identify issues, write review to /tmp/review.md
62: 
63: # Step 3: Codex fixes based on review
64: codex exec \
65:   "@/tmp/rate-limiter.ts Fix these issues: $(cat /tmp/review.md)" \
66:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/rate-limiter-v2.ts
67: ```
68: 
69: ### When to Use
70: 
71: - Code generation tasks where a second perspective catches edge cases
72: - Complex algorithms where verification matters more than speed
73: - Architecture decisions that benefit from adversarial review
74: 
75: ### Considerations
76: 
77: - Always validate the final output yourself (neither AI is infallible)
78: - Keep the review focused: bullet points of specific issues, not general feedback
79: - Limit to 2 fix cycles maximum; diminishing returns beyond that
80: 
81: ---
82: 
83: ## 3. JSON OUTPUT PROCESSING
84: 
85: **Extract structured data from Codex for programmatic use in the calling AI's workflows.**
86: 
87: ### Implementation
88: 
89: ```bash
90: # Request JSON explicitly in the prompt (Codex has no --output json flag)
91: codex exec \
92:   "Analyze src/auth.ts and return JSON with: {functions: [{name, params, returnType, complexity}], issues: [{line, severity, description}]}" \
93:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.json
94: 
95: # Parse with jq
96: jq '.issues[] | select(.severity == "high")' /tmp/analysis.json
97: 
98: # Parse with Node.js
99: node -e "
100: const fs = require('fs');
101: const raw = fs.readFileSync('/tmp/analysis.json', 'utf8');
102: // Codex outputs plain text; extract JSON from markdown code blocks if present
103: const jsonMatch = raw.match(/\`\`\`json\n([\s\S]*?)\n\`\`\`/) || raw.match(/(\{[\s\S]*\})/);
104: if (jsonMatch) {
105:   const parsed = JSON.parse(jsonMatch[1]);
106:   parsed.issues.filter(i => i.severity === 'high').forEach(i => {
107:     console.log(\`Line \${i.line}: \${i.description}\`);
108:   });
109: }
110: "
111: ```
112: 
113: ### Output Notes
114: 
115: Codex has no native JSON output wrapper — it outputs plain text to stdout. When requesting JSON:
116: 
117: - The model may wrap JSON in a markdown code block (` ```json ... ``` `)
118: - Strip the code fence before parsing with `jq` or `JSON.parse`
119: - Use explicit prompt instructions: "Return only raw JSON with no explanation or code fences."
120: 
121: ```bash
122: # Prompt that avoids code fences
123: codex exec \
124:   "Analyze src/auth.ts. Return ONLY raw JSON (no markdown, no explanation): {issues: [{line, severity, description}]}" \
125:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.json
126: 
127: jq '.issues' /tmp/analysis.json
128: ```
129: 
130: ### When to Use
131: 
132: - Extracting metrics, function signatures, or dependency lists
133: - Feeding Codex analysis into the calling AI's decision logic
134: - Building automated pipelines that branch on structured output
135: 
136: ---
137: 
138: ## 4. BACKGROUND EXECUTION
139: 
140: **Run Codex tasks in parallel while the calling AI continues working.**
141: 
142: ### Implementation
143: 
144: ```bash
145: # Launch multiple Codex tasks in background
146: codex exec "Review src/api/ for security vulnerabilities. Return JSON." \
147:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/security-review.txt 2>&1 &
148: PID1=$!
149: 
150: codex exec "Generate unit tests for src/utils.ts" \
151:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/generated-tests.ts 2>&1 &
152: PID2=$!
153: 
154: # Calling AI continues other work...
155: 
156: # Wait for specific task
157: wait $PID1
158: echo "Security review complete"
159: cat /tmp/security-review.txt | head -20
160: 
161: # Wait for all
162: wait $PID1 $PID2
163: echo "All Codex tasks complete"
164: ```
165: 
166: ### Monitoring
167: 
168: ```bash
169: # Check if still running
170: kill -0 $PID1 2>/dev/null && echo "Still running" || echo "Complete"
171: 
172: # Check output size (proxy for progress)
173: wc -c /tmp/security-review.txt
174: 
175: # Tail streaming output
176: tail -f /tmp/generated-tests.ts
177: ```
178: 
179: ### When to Use
180: 
181: - Independent tasks that do not depend on each other
182: - Long-running analysis while the calling AI handles quick edits
183: - Generating multiple artifacts simultaneously (tests, docs, types)
184: 
185: ### Considerations
186: 
187: - Always redirect stderr: `2>&1` to capture errors alongside output
188: - Set reasonable timeouts: `timeout 120 codex exec ...` to prevent hung processes
189: - Do not background tasks with `--sandbox workspace-write` or higher that write to the same files (race conditions)
190: - Background `--sandbox read-only` tasks are safe to parallelize freely
191: 
192: ### False-Completion Trap When Launching from Another AI's Bash Tool
193: 
194: When an orchestrating AI (Claude Code, Copilot, etc.) uses its `Bash` tool to launch `codex exec ... &`, the shell command returns exit 0 immediately because the `&` backgrounds the process and the parent shell exits. The orchestrating AI's task system reports "completed" even though the codex process is still running.
195: 
196: **Symptom:** All 5 parallel codex sessions "complete" in under 2 seconds. Output files are empty or missing.
197: 
198: **Root cause:** The Bash tool wraps the command in a subshell. `codex exec ... &` forks the process, the subshell exits, and the task system sees exit 0.
199: 
200: ```bash
201: # BAD: Reports instant "completion" to the orchestrator
202: codex exec "..." --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt &
203: echo "PID: $!"
204: # Shell exits immediately. Orchestrator thinks task is done.
205: 
206: # GOOD: Let the Bash tool wait for codex to finish
207: codex exec "..." --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt
208: # Bash tool blocks until codex completes. Use run_in_background on the Bash call itself.
209: ```
210: 
211: **Correct pattern for parallel codex from an orchestrating AI:**
212: 1. Launch each `codex exec` as a separate `Bash` call (no `&` suffix)
213: 2. Set `run_in_background: true` on each Bash tool call - this backgrounds the *tool call*, not the shell process
214: 3. The orchestrator gets notified when each codex process genuinely finishes
215: 4. Verify output files exist and have content before reading results
216: 
217: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
218: 
219: When a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input (e.g. a findings JSONL file) with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `codex exec ... &` inside the loop body, **codex silently consumes the loop's stdin**. The loop exits after the first 3-6 iterations with no error, dropping most dispatches.
220: 
221: **Symptom:** You dispatch a 27-finding batch; only 3-6 codex processes actually launch. No error, no warning. `ls *.pid | wc -l` returns a small number instead of the expected count.
222: 
223: **Root cause:** `codex exec` inherits the script's stdin by default. Because the `done < input.jsonl` redirection attaches the input file as the loop's stdin, each backgrounded codex process reads from that same file descriptor and races with the `read` command for lines — codex usually wins and consumes the remaining input.
224: 
225: ```bash
226: # BAD: codex inherits the loop's stdin, drains input.jsonl after iteration ~3
227: while IFS= read -r line; do
228:   codex exec "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
229:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
230: done < input.jsonl
231: # Result: 3 dispatches, 24 missing. No error output.
232: 
233: # GOOD: redirect codex stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
234: while IFS= read -r line; do
235:   codex exec "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
236:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
237: done < input.jsonl
238: # Result: all N dispatches launch cleanly.
239: ```
240: 
241: **When to remember this:**
242: - Any `while read ... done < file` or `while read ... done < <(cmd)` pattern that launches `codex exec` in its body.
243: - Any fan-out dispatcher that reads a per-finding / per-task / per-phase JSONL or list file and dispatches one codex per line.
244: - The bug is silent (no error), so you won't notice until you count `.pid` files or `applied/` reports and see a shortfall.
245: 
246: **Always pair `codex exec ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.** This is independent of whether codex itself uses stdin — the issue is shared FD consumption, not a feature.
247: 
248: ### Echoed-Transcript Parsing When Capturing `codex exec` Output
249: 
250: When you capture a `codex exec` transcript to a file and later parse it for structured output (a fenced JSON block, a verdict line, etc.), remember the transcript contains **three copies** of any marker your prompt mentions: (1) the **echoed prompt** itself — including any output-format template you embedded, with its literal placeholders; (2) the model's streamed answer; (3) the CLI **reprinting the final message** at the end.
251: 
252: **Symptom:** A parser that extracts text *between* the first and last marker concatenates all three blocks into invalid JSON (so your finding count comes out 0), and a global `grep` for a verdict/status line matches the **instruction line in the echoed prompt** (which usually lists every possible value), so you record the wrong one.
253: 
254: **Root cause:** `codex exec` echoes the full prompt and reprints its last message; any template token you put in the prompt reappears verbatim in the captured output.
255: 
256: ```bash
257: # BAD: between-markers awk spans the echoed template + answer + reprint
258: awk '/^===BLOCK===$/{f=1;next} /^===END===$/{f=0} f{print}' transcript.md   # → invalid JSON
259: grep -oE 'Verdict: (PASS|FAIL)' transcript.md | tail -1                      # → matches echoed instruction
260: 
261: # GOOD: collect EVERY fenced block, parse each independently, drop the
262: # placeholder echo (e.g. severity == "P0|P1|P2"), dedup, derive status from
263: # what survives. (Reference implementation: the run_review.sh driver under
264: # specs/.../123-deep-loop-parallel-fanout/008-deep-review/review/.)
265: ```
266: 
267: **Better still:** have codex write structured output with `-o lastmessage.txt`, or use a unique non-template sentinel the prompt never quotes. And always inspect one real captured transcript before trusting any count derived from it.
268: 
269: ---
270: 
271: ## 5. MODEL SELECTION STRATEGY
272: 
273: **Codex CLI supports 2 models. Choose based on task type.**
274: 
275: ### Decision Matrix
276: 
277: All tasks dispatch `--model gpt-5.5`. Tune reasoning effort per task type:
278: 
279: | Task Type | Reasoning Effort | Flag | Rationale |
280: |-----------|-----------------|------|-----------|
281: | Architecture analysis | `high` / `xhigh` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Complex analysis benefits from depth |
282: | Security audit | `high` / `xhigh` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Catches subtle vulnerability patterns |
283: | Complex planning | `high` / `xhigh` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Multi-strategy evaluation |
284: | Research synthesis | `high` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Better synthesis of findings |
285: | Code generation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Balanced for code output |
286: | Standard review | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Efficient pattern-based review |
287: | Implementation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Balanced for spec-to-code |
288: | Test generation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Solid test structure |
289: | Documentation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Efficient structured generation |
290: | Trivial lookups | `low` / `minimal` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="low"` | Minimize latency and cost |
291: 
292: ### Implementation
293: 
294: ```bash
295: # Reasoning-heavy tasks — raise reasoning_effort to high
296: codex exec "Review the authentication architecture for security gaps" \
297:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high"
298: 
299: codex exec "Plan the migration from REST to GraphQL" \
300:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high"
301: 
302: # Code-focused tasks — medium is fine
303: codex exec "Write tests for utils.ts" \
304:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium"
305: 
306: codex exec "Generate a rate limiter middleware" \
307:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium"
308: 
309: # Mixed workflow: analyze at high, implement at medium
310: codex exec "Analyze src/ for N+1 query patterns" \
311:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high" > /tmp/analysis.txt
312: 
313: codex exec "Fix the N+1 patterns identified: $(cat /tmp/analysis.txt)" \
314:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium"
315: ```
316: 
317: ### Why Explicit Model Specification Matters
318: 
319: - Omitting `--model` relies on the CLI default, which may change across Codex CLI versions
320: - Explicit specification ensures reproducible behavior in scripts and CI/CD pipelines
321: - The model can also be set in `.codex/config.toml` as a project-level default
322: 
323: ```toml
324: # .codex/config.toml - sets default for all invocations
325: model = "gpt-5.5"
326: model_reasoning_effort = "xhigh"
327: ```
328: 
329: ---
330: 
331: ## 6. SANDBOX STRATEGY
332: 
333: **Choose the least-permissive sandbox that allows the task to succeed.**
334: 
335: ### Decision Flow
336: 
337: ```
338: Task type?
339:   |
340:   +-- Analysis / review / exploration --> read-only
341:   |
342:   +-- Code generation / refactoring --> workspace-write
343:   |
344:   +-- System operations / migrations --> danger-full-access
345:                                           (+ --ask-for-approval untrusted)
346: ```
347: 
348: ### Implementation by Task Type
349: 
350: ```bash
351: # Analysis: read-only
352: codex exec "Identify all N+1 query patterns in src/" \
353:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5
354: 
355: # Code generation: workspace-write
356: codex exec "Add retry logic to all API calls in src/api/" \
357:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
358: 
359: # System migration: danger-full-access with explicit approval
360: codex exec "Migrate the database schema from v1 to v2" \
361:   --sandbox danger-full-access \
362:   --ask-for-approval untrusted \
363:   --model gpt-5.5
364: 
365: # Preview before committing: read-only first, workspace-write after review
366: codex exec "List all files that would be changed by the auth refactor" \
367:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/files-to-change.txt
368: # Review /tmp/files-to-change.txt, then proceed:
369: codex exec "@/tmp/files-to-change.txt Apply the auth refactor to these files" \
370:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
371: ```
372: 
373: ### Sandbox Combinations to Avoid
374: 
375: | Combination | Risk | Better Approach |
376: |-------------|------|-----------------|
377: | `danger-full-access` + `never` approval | Unrestricted, unreviewed changes | Pair with `untrusted` approval |
378: | `workspace-write` + blind background | Parallel writes to same files | Use `read-only` for parallel background tasks |
379: | `workspace-write` for pure analysis | Unnecessary permissions | Use `read-only`; it's sufficient for analysis |
380: 
381: ---
382: 
383: ## 7. CONTEXT ENRICHMENT
384: 
385: **Provide Codex with rich context for better results.**
386: 
387: ### @file References
388: 
389: ```bash
390: # Single file context
391: codex exec "@src/database.ts Refactor to use the repository pattern" \
392:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
393: 
394: # Multiple files for cross-file understanding
395: codex exec "@src/auth.ts @src/user.ts @src/session.ts These files have a circular dependency. Fix it." \
396:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
397: ```
398: 
399: ### Project Context via instructions.md
400: 
401: Create `.codex/instructions.md` to persist context across all Codex sessions:
402: 
403: ```markdown
404: # Project Context
405: 
406: ## Architecture
407: - TypeScript monorepo, Express.js + PostgreSQL (Prisma ORM)
408: - JWT authentication with refresh token rotation
409: 
410: ## Conventions
411: - Functional style; avoid classes except for Error types
412: - All public exports must have JSDoc
413: - Use Result<T, E> pattern for error handling
414: 
415: ## Do Not
416: - Modify prisma/schema.prisma without explicit instruction
417: - Add npm dependencies without justification
418: ```
419: 
420: ### Explicit Context Injection
421: 
422: ```bash
423: # Inject the calling AI's analysis as context
424: CLAUDE_ANALYSIS="The bug is in the token refresh logic. The refresh token
425: is not being rotated on use, allowing token replay attacks."
426: 
427: codex exec \
428:   "@src/auth/tokens.ts Fix this security issue. Context from prior analysis: $CLAUDE_ANALYSIS" \
429:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
430: ```
431: 
432: ### Web Search for Current Information
433: 
434: ```bash
435: # Enable live web browsing with --search
436: codex --search exec \
437:   "Research the current best practices for refresh token rotation in Express.js. Implement the recommended pattern in src/auth/tokens.ts" \
438:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
439: ```
440: 
441: ---
442: 
443: ## 8. VALIDATION PIPELINE
444: 
445: **Multi-stage validation of Codex-generated output.**
446: 
447: ### Implementation
448: 
449: ```bash
450: # Stage 1: Generate
451: codex exec "Create a webhook handler for Stripe events" \
452:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/webhook.ts
453: 
454: # Stage 2: Syntax check
455: npx tsc --noEmit /tmp/webhook.ts 2>/tmp/syntax-errors.txt
456: if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
457:   codex exec \
458:     "@/tmp/webhook.ts Fix these TypeScript errors: $(cat /tmp/syntax-errors.txt)" \
459:     --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/webhook-fixed.ts
460:   cp /tmp/webhook-fixed.ts /tmp/webhook.ts
461: fi
462: 
463: # Stage 3: Security scan
464: codex exec \
465:   "@/tmp/webhook.ts Audit this code for security issues. Focus on: input validation, injection attacks, authentication bypasses. Return JSON: {issues: [{severity, line, description, fix}]}" \
466:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/security-scan.txt
467: 
468: # Stage 4: Functional check (calling AI reviews the result)
469: # Read /tmp/webhook.ts and /tmp/security-scan.txt within the calling AI
470: 
471: # Stage 5: Style alignment
472: codex exec \
473:   "@/tmp/webhook.ts Reformat to match project conventions. Functional style, Result<T,E> error handling, JSDoc on exports." \
474:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/webhook-final.ts
475: ```
476: 
477: ### Pipeline Stages (Recommended Order)
478: 
479: | Stage | Purpose | Tool |
480: |-------|---------|------|
481: | 1. Generate | Create initial artifact | Codex (`gpt-5.5` @ `medium`, `workspace-write`) |
482: | 2. Syntax | Verify it compiles/parses | Language toolchain (tsc, eslint, etc.) |
483: | 3. Security | Check for vulnerabilities | Codex (`gpt-5.5` @ `high`, `read-only`) |
484: | 4. Functional | Verify correctness | Calling AI review or tests |
485: | 5. Style | Match project conventions | Codex (`gpt-5.5` @ `medium`, `workspace-write`) |
486: 
487: ### When to Use
488: 
489: - Any generated code that will be committed to the repository
490: - Security-sensitive code (auth, payments, data handling)
491: - Code that lacks test coverage
492: 
493: ---
494: 
495: ## 9. INCREMENTAL REFINEMENT
496: 
497: **Build complex artifacts in stages, verifying each stage before proceeding.**
498: 
499: ### Implementation
500: 
501: ```bash
502: # Stage 1: Type definitions (read-only analysis + workspace-write output)
503: codex exec \
504:   "Create the type definitions and function signatures for a task queue system. Types only, no implementation. Export all types." \
505:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > src/task-queue/types.ts
506: 
507: # Verify stage 1
508: npx tsc --noEmit src/task-queue/types.ts
509: 
510: # Stage 2: Core implementation
511: codex exec \
512:   "@src/task-queue/types.ts Implement the core TaskQueue class using these types. Handle enqueue, dequeue, retry with exponential backoff." \
513:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > src/task-queue/queue.ts
514: 
515: # Verify stage 2
516: npx tsc --noEmit src/task-queue/queue.ts
517: 
518: # Stage 3: Tests
519: codex exec \
520:   "@src/task-queue/types.ts @src/task-queue/queue.ts Write comprehensive tests for the TaskQueue. Cover: enqueue, dequeue, retry logic, concurrency limits, error handling." \
521:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > src/task-queue/__tests__/queue.test.ts
522: 
523: # Verify stage 3
524: npx jest src/task-queue/__tests__/queue.test.ts
525: ```
526: 
527: ### Stage Progression Rules
528: 
529: 1. Never proceed to the next stage if the current stage has errors.
530: 2. Each stage gets the output of all previous stages as `@file` context.
531: 3. Keep stages small enough that they can be fully reviewed.
532: 4. Use `gpt-5.5` for all stages; tune reasoning effort per stage (e.g., `high` for design, `medium` for implementation).
533: 
534: ### When to Use
535: 
536: - Building new modules or subsystems from scratch
537: - Complex features with multiple interacting components
538: - When you want to maintain control over architectural decisions at each step
539: 
540: ---
541: 
542: ## 10. CROSS-VALIDATION WITH CLAUDE
543: 
544: **Use both AIs to validate each other's work, leveraging different strengths.**
545: 
546: ### Claude Generates, Codex Reviews
547: 
548: ```bash
549: # Calling AI generates code (within the session)
550: # Then Codex reviews it:
551: codex exec \
552:   "@src/newly-generated-module.ts Review this code for: correctness, edge cases, performance issues, and adherence to SOLID principles. Be critical. Return findings as JSON." \
553:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/codex-review.txt
554: ```
555: 
556: ### Codex Generates, Claude Reviews
557: 
558: ```bash
559: # Codex generates
560: codex exec "Create a caching layer with TTL support and LRU eviction" \
561:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/cache.ts
562: 
563: # Calling AI reviews within the session (read /tmp/cache.ts and analyze)
564: ```
565: 
566: ### Strength Comparison for Task Routing
567: 
568: | Strength Area | Calling AI | Codex CLI |
569: |---------------|-------------|-----------|
570: | Codebase context | Deep (built-in tools, spec-folder continuity docs) | Good (with @file references) |
571: | Web search | Via web search tool | Via `--search` flag |
572: | Multi-file refactoring | Strong | Strong |
573: | Architecture reasoning | Strong | Strong (xhigh reasoning) |
574: | Sandbox-isolated execution | No (direct file access) | Yes (enforced by sandbox mode) |
575: | Session continuity | Built-in (conversation context) | Via `codex resume` / `codex fork` |
576: | Spec-folder continuity | Native | Not available |
577: | Real-time information | Via web search tool | Via `--search` flag |
578: 
579: ### Cross-Validation Strategies
580: 
581: | Strategy | Flow | Best For |
582: |----------|------|----------|
583: | **Adversarial review** | A generates, B critiques | Security-critical code |
584: | **Consensus check** | Both solve independently, compare | Architectural decisions |
585: | **Specialist routing** | Route by strength (table above) | Efficiency optimization |
586: | **Red team** | A writes, B tries to break | Auth, payments, data access |
587: | **Sandbox isolation** | Codex generates in sandboxed environment | Risky migrations or system changes |
588: 
589: ---
590: 
591: ## 11. SESSION CONTINUITY
592: 
593: **Maintain context across multiple Codex invocations for complex, multi-turn tasks.**
594: 
595: ### Session Operations
596: 
597: ```bash
598: # Resume a previous session (interactive TUI)
599: codex resume
600: 
601: # Resume a specific session by ID
602: codex resume <session-id>
603: 
604: # Fork a session before a risky operation (creates a branch)
605: codex fork <session-id>
606: 
607: # Non-interactive resume and continue
608: codex exec --session-id <id> \
609:   "Continue implementing the rate limiter from where we left off" \
610:   --model gpt-5.5
611: ```
612: 
613: ### Multi-Turn Scripted Workflow
614: 
615: ```bash
616: # Turn 1: Analysis - capture session ID from output if available
617: codex exec "Analyze src/auth/ architecture. List 5 improvements." \
618:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.txt
619: # Note the session ID displayed in TUI or output
620: 
621: # Turn 2: Implement first improvement (in same session)
622: SESSION_ID="<id-from-turn-1>"
623: codex exec --session-id "$SESSION_ID" \
624:   "Implement improvement #1 from your analysis" \
625:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
626: 
627: # Fork before trying a risky approach
628: codex fork "$SESSION_ID"
629: FORK_ID="<fork-id>"
630: codex exec --session-id "$FORK_ID" \
631:   "Attempt the aggressive refactor approach" \
632:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
633: ```
634: 
635: ### When to Use Each Operation
636: 
637: | Operation | When to Use |
638: |-----------|-------------|
639: | `resume` | Continue a multi-step task with existing Codex context |
640: | `fork` | Try a different approach without losing the original session state |
641: | New session | Fresh context; prior session is not relevant |
642: | `codex exec` (stateless) | One-shot tasks; simpler to re-provide context than manage sessions |
643: 
644: ### Considerations
645: 
646: - For cross-AI orchestration, it is often simpler to re-provide context via `@file` references than to manage session IDs across multiple `codex exec` calls.
647: - Use sessions when the task genuinely builds on prior Codex reasoning that would be costly to re-establish.
648: - Fork before any operation that could leave the session in a broken state.
649: 
650: ---
651: 
652: ## 12. ANTI-PATTERNS
653: 
654: **What NOT to do when orchestrating Codex CLI from the calling AI.**
655: 
656: ### 1. Using --full-auto Without Review
657: 
658: ```bash
659: # BAD: Full-auto on destructive operations
660: codex exec "Clean up the codebase" --full-auto  # May delete or alter files unexpectedly
661: 
662: # GOOD: Review plan first, then execute specific steps
663: codex exec "List files that could be cleaned up. Do not delete anything." \
664:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5
665: # Review the list, then selectively execute
666: ```
667: 
668: ### 2. Using danger-full-access Without Approval
669: 
670: ```bash
671: # BAD: Unrestricted access with no human checkpoint
672: codex exec "Migrate the database" \
673:   --sandbox danger-full-access --ask-for-approval never --model gpt-5.5
674: 
675: # GOOD: Full access with explicit approval required
676: codex exec "Migrate the database" \
677:   --sandbox danger-full-access --ask-for-approval untrusted --model gpt-5.5
678: ```
679: 
680: ### 3. Trusting Output Blindly
681: 
682: ```bash
683: # BAD: Direct pipe to production
684: codex exec "Generate migration SQL" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
685:   | psql production_db
686: 
687: # GOOD: Generate, review, test, then apply
688: codex exec "Generate migration SQL" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
689:   > /tmp/migration.sql
690: # Review /tmp/migration.sql
691: # Test on staging: psql staging_db -f /tmp/migration.sql
692: # Then apply to production
693: ```
694: 
695: ### 4. Over-Specifying in a Single Prompt
696: 
697: ```bash
698: # BAD: Everything at once
699: codex exec "Create a complete REST API with auth, CRUD for users/posts/comments, \
700:   rate limiting, caching, logging, monitoring, tests, and deployment config" \
701:   --model gpt-5.5
702: 
703: # GOOD: Incremental (Pattern 9)
704: codex exec "Create type definitions for a blog API: User, Post, Comment" \
705:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
706: # Then build on top incrementally
707: ```
708: 
709: ### 5. Background Tasks Writing the Same Files
710: 
711: ```bash
712: # BAD: Parallel writes to overlapping files
713: codex exec "Fix auth" --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 &
714: codex exec "Fix auth tests" --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 &
715: # Race condition: both modify src/auth/ simultaneously
716: 
717: # GOOD: Background only for independent, read-only analysis
718: codex exec "Review src/auth/" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
719:   > /tmp/auth-review.txt &
720: codex exec "Review src/payments/" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
721:   > /tmp/pay-review.txt &
722: wait
723: ```
724: 
725: ### 6. Using --oss for Production Workflows
726: 
727: ```bash
728: # BAD: OSS models in automated pipelines (unpredictable quality)
729: codex exec "Fix the authentication bug" --oss --model gpt-5.5
730: 
731: # GOOD: Use --oss only for local experimentation
732: # For production workflows, always use gpt-5.5 with ChatGPT OAuth (codex login)
733: codex exec "Fix the authentication bug" --model gpt-5.5
734: ```
735: 
736: ### 7. Backgrounding codex exec Inside Shell Scripts Called by Another AI
737: 
738: ```bash
739: # BAD: & inside the shell command - orchestrator sees instant exit 0
740: codex exec "Deep review all phases" --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt 2>&1 &
741: echo "PID: $!"
742: # The Bash tool reports "completed" in <2 seconds. Codex is still running.
743: 
744: # GOOD: No & - use the orchestrator's own background mechanism instead
745: # In Claude Code: Bash(command="codex exec ...", run_in_background=true)
746: # In Copilot: background delegation
747: # The orchestrator waits for the actual codex process to finish.
748: codex exec "Deep review all phases" --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt 2>&1
749: ```
750: 
751: This is the most common false-completion trap in cross-AI orchestration. The orchestrating AI reads empty output files and either hallucinates results or reports stale data from a prior run.
752: 
753: ### 8. Forgetting Context in Stateless exec Calls
754: 
755: ```bash
756: # BAD: Follow-up without re-providing context
757: codex exec "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model gpt-5.5  # Turn 1
758: codex exec "Now fix the issue you found" --model gpt-5.5  # Turn 2: Codex has no memory of Turn 1
759: 
760: # GOOD: Re-provide context or use session resume
761: codex exec "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.txt
762: codex exec "@src/auth.ts Fix the issues identified: $(cat /tmp/analysis.txt)" \
763:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
764: ```

15: 
16: # Cross-AI Orchestration Patterns: Calling AI + Codex CLI
17: 
18: Proven patterns for orchestrating Codex CLI from any AI assistant session.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Core Principle
25: 
26: The calling AI acts as the orchestrator (planner, validator, integrator) while Codex CLI executes targeted tasks. The value comes from combining different model perspectives and leveraging Codex's sandbox-controlled execution, not from redundant work.
27: 
28: ### Purpose
29: 
30: Each pattern documented here includes the rationale, implementation template, and practical considerations for combining the calling AI with Codex CLI effectively.
31: 
32: ### When to Use
33: 
34: - You need a second AI perspective on generated code, architecture, or security
35: - Codex's strengths (sandbox isolation, `xhigh` reasoning, web search via `--search`) complement the calling AI's strengths
36: - You want to run parallel AI tasks while the calling AI continues working
37: - Complex workflows benefit from structured, multi-stage generation and validation
38: - You need controlled file modification with sandbox-enforced safety boundaries
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## 2. GENERATE-REVIEW-FIX CYCLE
43: 
44: **The most reliable cross-AI pattern.** One AI generates, the other reviews, then the original fixes.
45: 
46: ### Flow
47: 
48: ```
49: Calling AI (plan) --> Codex CLI (generate) --> Calling AI (review) --> Codex CLI (fix)
50: ```
51: 
52: ### Implementation
53: 
54: ```bash
55: # Step 1: Codex generates the code
56: codex exec \
57:   "Create a rate limiter middleware for Express with sliding window algorithm. Output only the code, no explanation." \
58:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/rate-limiter.ts
59: 
60: # Step 2: Calling AI reviews (done within the calling AI session)
61: # Read /tmp/rate-limiter.ts, identify issues, write review to /tmp/review.md
62: 
63: # Step 3: Codex fixes based on review
64: codex exec \
65:   "@/tmp/rate-limiter.ts Fix these issues: $(cat /tmp/review.md)" \
66:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/rate-limiter-v2.ts
67: ```
68: 
69: ### When to Use
70: 
71: - Code generation tasks where a second perspective catches edge cases
72: - Complex algorithms where verification matters more than speed
73: - Architecture decisions that benefit from adversarial review
74: 
75: ### Considerations
76: 
77: - Always validate the final output yourself (neither AI is infallible)
78: - Keep the review focused: bullet points of specific issues, not general feedback
79: - Limit to 2 fix cycles maximum; diminishing returns beyond that
80: 
81: ---
82: 
83: ## 3. JSON OUTPUT PROCESSING
84: 
85: **Extract structured data from Codex for programmatic use in the calling AI's workflows.**
86: 
87: ### Implementation
88: 
89: ```bash
90: # Request JSON explicitly in the prompt (Codex has no --output json flag)
91: codex exec \
92:   "Analyze src/auth.ts and return JSON with: {functions: [{name, params, returnType, complexity}], issues: [{line, severity, description}]}" \
93:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.json
94: 
95: # Parse with jq
96: jq '.issues[] | select(.severity == "high")' /tmp/analysis.json
97: 
98: # Parse with Node.js
99: node -e "
100: const fs = require('fs');
101: const raw = fs.readFileSync('/tmp/analysis.json', 'utf8');
102: // Codex outputs plain text; extract JSON from markdown code blocks if present
103: const jsonMatch = raw.match(/\`\`\`json\n([\s\S]*?)\n\`\`\`/) || raw.match(/(\{[\s\S]*\})/);
104: if (jsonMatch) {
105:   const parsed = JSON.parse(jsonMatch[1]);
106:   parsed.issues.filter(i => i.severity === 'high').forEach(i => {
107:     console.log(\`Line \${i.line}: \${i.description}\`);
108:   });
109: }
110: "
111: ```
112: 
113: ### Output Notes
114: 
115: Codex has no native JSON output wrapper — it outputs plain text to stdout. When requesting JSON:
116: 
117: - The model may wrap JSON in a markdown code block (` ```json ... ``` `)
118: - Strip the code fence before parsing with `jq` or `JSON.parse`
119: - Use explicit prompt instructions: "Return only raw JSON with no explanation or code fences."
120: 
121: ```bash
122: # Prompt that avoids code fences
123: codex exec \
124:   "Analyze src/auth.ts. Return ONLY raw JSON (no markdown, no explanation): {issues: [{line, severity, description}]}" \
125:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.json
126: 
127: jq '.issues' /tmp/analysis.json
128: ```
129: 
130: ### When to Use
131: 
132: - Extracting metrics, function signatures, or dependency lists
133: - Feeding Codex analysis into the calling AI's decision logic
134: - Building automated pipelines that branch on structured output
135: 
136: ---
137: 
138: ## 4. BACKGROUND EXECUTION
139: 
140: **Run Codex tasks in parallel while the calling AI continues working.**
141: 
142: ### Implementation
143: 
144: ```bash
145: # Launch multiple Codex tasks in background
146: codex exec "Review src/api/ for security vulnerabilities. Return JSON." \
147:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/security-review.txt 2>&1 &
148: PID1=$!
149: 
150: codex exec "Generate unit tests for src/utils.ts" \
151:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/generated-tests.ts 2>&1 &
152: PID2=$!
153: 
154: # Calling AI continues other work...
155: 
156: # Wait for specific task
157: wait $PID1
158: echo "Security review complete"
159: cat /tmp/security-review.txt | head -20
160: 
161: # Wait for all
162: wait $PID1 $PID2
163: echo "All Codex tasks complete"
164: ```
165: 
166: ### Monitoring
167: 
168: ```bash
169: # Check if still running
170: kill -0 $PID1 2>/dev/null && echo "Still running" || echo "Complete"
171: 
172: # Check output size (proxy for progress)
173: wc -c /tmp/security-review.txt
174: 
175: # Tail streaming output
176: tail -f /tmp/generated-tests.ts
177: ```
178: 
179: ### When to Use
180: 
181: - Independent tasks that do not depend on each other
182: - Long-running analysis while the calling AI handles quick edits
183: - Generating multiple artifacts simultaneously (tests, docs, types)
184: 
185: ### Considerations
186: 
187: - Always redirect stderr: `2>&1` to capture errors alongside output
188: - Set reasonable timeouts: `timeout 120 codex exec ...` to prevent hung processes
189: - Do not background tasks with `--sandbox workspace-write` or higher that write to the same files (race conditions)
190: - Background `--sandbox read-only` tasks are safe to parallelize freely
191: 
192: ### False-Completion Trap When Launching from Another AI's Bash Tool
193: 
194: When an orchestrating AI (Claude Code, Copilot, etc.) uses its `Bash` tool to launch `codex exec ... &`, the shell command returns exit 0 immediately because the `&` backgrounds the process and the parent shell exits. The orchestrating AI's task system reports "completed" even though the codex process is still running.
195: 
196: **Symptom:** All 5 parallel codex sessions "complete" in under 2 seconds. Output files are empty or missing.
197: 
198: **Root cause:** The Bash tool wraps the command in a subshell. `codex exec ... &` forks the process, the subshell exits, and the task system sees exit 0.
199: 
200: ```bash
201: # BAD: Reports instant "completion" to the orchestrator
202: codex exec "..." --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt &
203: echo "PID: $!"
204: # Shell exits immediately. Orchestrator thinks task is done.
205: 
206: # GOOD: Let the Bash tool wait for codex to finish
207: codex exec "..." --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt
208: # Bash tool blocks until codex completes. Use run_in_background on the Bash call itself.
209: ```
210: 
211: **Correct pattern for parallel codex from an orchestrating AI:**
212: 1. Launch each `codex exec` as a separate `Bash` call (no `&` suffix)
213: 2. Set `run_in_background: true` on each Bash tool call - this backgrounds the *tool call*, not the shell process
214: 3. The orchestrator gets notified when each codex process genuinely finishes
215: 4. Verify output files exist and have content before reading results
216: 
217: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
218: 
219: When a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input (e.g. a findings JSONL file) with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `codex exec ... &` inside the loop body, **codex silently consumes the loop's stdin**. The loop exits after the first 3-6 iterations with no error, dropping most dispatches.
220: 
221: **Symptom:** You dispatch a 27-finding batch; only 3-6 codex processes actually launch. No error, no warning. `ls *.pid | wc -l` returns a small number instead of the expected count.
222: 
223: **Root cause:** `codex exec` inherits the script's stdin by default. Because the `done < input.jsonl` redirection attaches the input file as the loop's stdin, each backgrounded codex process reads from that same file descriptor and races with the `read` command for lines — codex usually wins and consumes the remaining input.
224: 
225: ```bash
226: # BAD: codex inherits the loop's stdin, drains input.jsonl after iteration ~3
227: while IFS= read -r line; do
228:   codex exec "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
229:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
230: done < input.jsonl
231: # Result: 3 dispatches, 24 missing. No error output.
232: 
233: # GOOD: redirect codex stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
234: while IFS= read -r line; do
235:   codex exec "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
236:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
237: done < input.jsonl
238: # Result: all N dispatches launch cleanly.
239: ```
240: 
241: **When to remember this:**
242: - Any `while read ... done < file` or `while read ... done < <(cmd)` pattern that launches `codex exec` in its body.
243: - Any fan-out dispatcher that reads a per-finding / per-task / per-phase JSONL or list file and dispatches one codex per line.
244: - The bug is silent (no error), so you won't notice until you count `.pid` files or `applied/` reports and see a shortfall.
245: 
246: **Always pair `codex exec ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.** This is independent of whether codex itself uses stdin — the issue is shared FD consumption, not a feature.
247: 
248: ### Echoed-Transcript Parsing When Capturing `codex exec` Output
249: 
250: When you capture a `codex exec` transcript to a file and later parse it for structured output (a fenced JSON block, a verdict line, etc.), remember the transcript contains **three copies** of any marker your prompt mentions: (1) the **echoed prompt** itself — including any output-format template you embedded, with its literal placeholders; (2) the model's streamed answer; (3) the CLI **reprinting the final message** at the end.
251: 
252: **Symptom:** A parser that extracts text *between* the first and last marker concatenates all three blocks into invalid JSON (so your finding count comes out 0), and a global `grep` for a verdict/status line matches the **instruction line in the echoed prompt** (which usually lists every possible value), so you record the wrong one.
253: 
254: **Root cause:** `codex exec` echoes the full prompt and reprints its last message; any template token you put in the prompt reappears verbatim in the captured output.
255: 
256: ```bash
257: # BAD: between-markers awk spans the echoed template + answer + reprint
258: awk '/^===BLOCK===$/{f=1;next} /^===END===$/{f=0} f{print}' transcript.md   # → invalid JSON
259: grep -oE 'Verdict: (PASS|FAIL)' transcript.md | tail -1                      # → matches echoed instruction
260: 
261: # GOOD: collect EVERY fenced block, parse each independently, drop the
262: # placeholder echo (e.g. severity == "P0|P1|P2"), dedup, derive status from
263: # what survives. (Reference implementation: the run_review.sh driver under
264: # specs/.../123-deep-loop-parallel-fanout/008-deep-review/review/.)
265: ```
266: 
267: **Better still:** have codex write structured output with `-o lastmessage.txt`, or use a unique non-template sentinel the prompt never quotes. And always inspect one real captured transcript before trusting any count derived from it.
268: 
269: ---
270: 
271: ## 5. MODEL SELECTION STRATEGY
272: 
273: **Codex CLI supports 2 models. Choose based on task type.**
274: 
275: ### Decision Matrix
276: 
277: All tasks dispatch `--model gpt-5.5`. Tune reasoning effort per task type:
278: 
279: | Task Type | Reasoning Effort | Flag | Rationale |
280: |-----------|-----------------|------|-----------|
281: | Architecture analysis | `high` / `xhigh` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Complex analysis benefits from depth |
282: | Security audit | `high` / `xhigh` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Catches subtle vulnerability patterns |
283: | Complex planning | `high` / `xhigh` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Multi-strategy evaluation |
284: | Research synthesis | `high` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | Better synthesis of findings |
285: | Code generation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Balanced for code output |
286: | Standard review | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Efficient pattern-based review |
287: | Implementation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Balanced for spec-to-code |
288: | Test generation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Solid test structure |
289: | Documentation | `medium` (default) | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` | Efficient structured generation |
290: | Trivial lookups | `low` / `minimal` | `-c model_reasoning_effort="low"` | Minimize latency and cost |
291: 
292: ### Implementation
293: 
294: ```bash
295: # Reasoning-heavy tasks — raise reasoning_effort to high
296: codex exec "Review the authentication architecture for security gaps" \
297:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high"
298: 
299: codex exec "Plan the migration from REST to GraphQL" \
300:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high"
301: 
302: # Code-focused tasks — medium is fine
303: codex exec "Write tests for utils.ts" \
304:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium"
305: 
306: codex exec "Generate a rate limiter middleware" \
307:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium"
308: 
309: # Mixed workflow: analyze at high, implement at medium
310: codex exec "Analyze src/ for N+1 query patterns" \
311:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high" > /tmp/analysis.txt
312: 
313: codex exec "Fix the N+1 patterns identified: $(cat /tmp/analysis.txt)" \
314:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium"
315: ```
316: 
317: ### Why Explicit Model Specification Matters
318: 
319: - Omitting `--model` relies on the CLI default, which may change across Codex CLI versions
320: - Explicit specification ensures reproducible behavior in scripts and CI/CD pipelines
321: - The model can also be set in `.codex/config.toml` as a project-level default
322: 
323: ```toml
324: # .codex/config.toml - sets default for all invocations
325: model = "gpt-5.5"
326: model_reasoning_effort = "xhigh"
327: ```
328: 
329: ---
330: 
331: ## 6. SANDBOX STRATEGY
332: 
333: **Choose the least-permissive sandbox that allows the task to succeed.**
334: 
335: ### Decision Flow
336: 
337: ```
338: Task type?
339:   |
340:   +-- Analysis / review / exploration --> read-only
341:   |
342:   +-- Code generation / refactoring --> workspace-write
343:   |
344:   +-- System operations / migrations --> danger-full-access
345:                                           (+ --ask-for-approval untrusted)
346: ```
347: 
348: ### Implementation by Task Type
349: 
350: ```bash
351: # Analysis: read-only
352: codex exec "Identify all N+1 query patterns in src/" \
353:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5
354: 
355: # Code generation: workspace-write
356: codex exec "Add retry logic to all API calls in src/api/" \
357:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
358: 
359: # System migration: danger-full-access with explicit approval

361:   --sandbox danger-full-access \
362:   --ask-for-approval untrusted \
363:   --model gpt-5.5

366: codex exec "List all files that would be changed by the auth refactor" \
367:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/files-to-change.txt

376: |-------------|------|-----------------|

378: | `workspace-write` + blind background | Parallel writes to same files | Use `read-only` for parallel background tasks |
379: | `workspace-write` for pure analysis | Unnecessary permissions | Use `read-only`; it's sufficient for analysis |

479: | Stage | Purpose | Tool |
480: |-------|---------|------|

482: | 2. Syntax | Verify it compiles/parses | Language toolchain (tsc, eslint, etc.) |
483: | 3. Security | Check for vulnerabilities | Codex (`gpt-5.5` @ `high`, `read-only`) |

487: ### When to Use

489: - Any generated code that will be committed to the repository
490: - Security-sensitive code (auth, payments, data handling)
491: - Code that lacks test coverage

495: ## 9. INCREMENTAL REFINEMENT
496: 
497: **Build complex artifacts in stages, verifying each stage before proceeding.**
498: 
499: ### Implementation
500: 
501: ```bash

503: codex exec \
504:   "Create the type definitions and function signatures for a task queue system. Types only, no implementation. Export all types." \
505:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > src/task-queue/types.ts
506: 
507: # Verify stage 1
508: npx tsc --noEmit src/task-queue/types.ts

511: codex exec \
512:   "@src/task-queue/types.ts Implement the core TaskQueue class using these types. Handle enqueue, dequeue, retry with exponential backoff." \

516: npx tsc --noEmit src/task-queue/queue.ts

521:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > src/task-queue/__tests__/queue.test.ts

529: 1. Never proceed to the next stage if the current stage has errors.
530: 2. Each stage gets the output of all previous stages as `@file` context.
531: 3. Keep stages small enough that they can be fully reviewed.
532: 4. Use `gpt-5.5` for all stages; tune reasoning effort per stage (e.g., `high` for design, `medium` for implementation).

534: ### When to Use

536: - Building new modules or subsystems from scratch
537: - Complex features with multiple interacting components
538: - When you want to maintain control over architectural decisions at each step

542: ## 10. CROSS-VALIDATION WITH CLAUDE
543: 
544: **Use both AIs to validate each other's work, leveraging different strengths.**
545: 
546: ### Claude Generates, Codex Reviews
547: 
548: ```bash
549: # Calling AI generates code (within the session)
550: # Then Codex reviews it:
551: codex exec \
552:   "@src/newly-generated-module.ts Review this code for: correctness, edge cases, performance issues, and adherence to SOLID principles. Be critical. Return findings as JSON." \
553:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/codex-review.txt
554: ```
555: 
556: ### Codex Generates, Claude Reviews
557: 
558: ```bash
559: # Codex generates
560: codex exec "Create a caching layer with TTL support and LRU eviction" \
561:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/cache.ts
562: 
563: # Calling AI reviews within the session (read /tmp/cache.ts and analyze)
564: ```
565: 
566: ### Strength Comparison for Task Routing
567: 
568: | Strength Area | Calling AI | Codex CLI |
569: |---------------|-------------|-----------|
570: | Codebase context | Deep (built-in tools, spec-folder continuity docs) | Good (with @file references) |
571: | Web search | Via web search tool | Via `--search` flag |
572: | Multi-file refactoring | Strong | Strong |
573: | Architecture reasoning | Strong | Strong (xhigh reasoning) |
574: | Sandbox-isolated execution | No (direct file access) | Yes (enforced by sandbox mode) |
575: | Session continuity | Built-in (conversation context) | Via `codex resume` / `codex fork` |
576: | Spec-folder continuity | Native | Not available |
577: | Real-time information | Via web search tool | Via `--search` flag |
578: 
579: ### Cross-Validation Strategies
580: 
581: | Strategy | Flow | Best For |
582: |----------|------|----------|
583: | **Adversarial review** | A generates, B critiques | Security-critical code |
584: | **Consensus check** | Both solve independently, compare | Architectural decisions |
585: | **Specialist routing** | Route by strength (table above) | Efficiency optimization |
586: | **Red team** | A writes, B tries to break | Auth, payments, data access |
587: | **Sandbox isolation** | Codex generates in sandboxed environment | Risky migrations or system changes |

589: ---
590: 
591: ## 11. SESSION CONTINUITY
592: 
593: **Maintain context across multiple Codex invocations for complex, multi-turn tasks.**
594: 
595: ### Session Operations
596: 
597: ```bash
598: # Resume a previous session (interactive TUI)
599: codex resume
600: 
601: # Resume a specific session by ID
602: codex resume <session-id>
603: 
604: # Fork a session before a risky operation (creates a branch)
605: codex fork <session-id>
606: 
607: # Non-interactive resume and continue
608: codex exec --session-id <id> \
609:   "Continue implementing the rate limiter from where we left off" \
610:   --model gpt-5.5
611: ```
612: 
613: ### Multi-Turn Scripted Workflow
614: 
615: ```bash
616: # Turn 1: Analysis - capture session ID from output if available
617: codex exec "Analyze src/auth/ architecture. List 5 improvements." \
618:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.txt
619: # Note the session ID displayed in TUI or output
620: 
621: # Turn 2: Implement first improvement (in same session)
622: SESSION_ID="<id-from-turn-1>"
623: codex exec --session-id "$SESSION_ID" \
624:   "Implement improvement #1 from your analysis" \
625:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
626: 
627: # Fork before trying a risky approach
628: codex fork "$SESSION_ID"
629: FORK_ID="<fork-id>"
630: codex exec --session-id "$FORK_ID" \
631:   "Attempt the aggressive refactor approach" \
632:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
633: ```
634: 
635: ### When to Use Each Operation
636: 
637: | Operation | When to Use |
638: |-----------|-------------|
639: | `resume` | Continue a multi-step task with existing Codex context |
640: | `fork` | Try a different approach without losing the original session state |
641: | New session | Fresh context; prior session is not relevant |
642: | `codex exec` (stateless) | One-shot tasks; simpler to re-provide context than manage sessions |
643: 
644: ### Considerations
645: 
646: - For cross-AI orchestration, it is often simpler to re-provide context via `@file` references than to manage session IDs across multiple `codex exec` calls.
647: - Use sessions when the task genuinely builds on prior Codex reasoning that would be costly to re-establish.
648: - Fork before any operation that could leave the session in a broken state.
649: 
650: ---
651: 
652: ## 12. ANTI-PATTERNS
653: 
654: **What NOT to do when orchestrating Codex CLI from the calling AI.**
655: 
656: ### 1. Using --full-auto Without Review
657: 
658: ```bash
659: # BAD: Full-auto on destructive operations
660: codex exec "Clean up the codebase" --full-auto  # May delete or alter files unexpectedly
661: 
662: # GOOD: Review plan first, then execute specific steps
663: codex exec "List files that could be cleaned up. Do not delete anything." \
664:   --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5
665: # Review the list, then selectively execute
666: ```
667: 
668: ### 2. Using danger-full-access Without Approval
669: 
670: ```bash
671: # BAD: Unrestricted access with no human checkpoint
672: codex exec "Migrate the database" \
673:   --sandbox danger-full-access --ask-for-approval never --model gpt-5.5
674: 
675: # GOOD: Full access with explicit approval required
676: codex exec "Migrate the database" \
677:   --sandbox danger-full-access --ask-for-approval untrusted --model gpt-5.5
678: ```
679: 
680: ### 3. Trusting Output Blindly
681: 
682: ```bash
683: # BAD: Direct pipe to production
684: codex exec "Generate migration SQL" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
685:   | psql production_db
686: 
687: # GOOD: Generate, review, test, then apply
688: codex exec "Generate migration SQL" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
689:   > /tmp/migration.sql
690: # Review /tmp/migration.sql
691: # Test on staging: psql staging_db -f /tmp/migration.sql
692: # Then apply to production
693: ```
694: 
695: ### 4. Over-Specifying in a Single Prompt
696: 
697: ```bash
698: # BAD: Everything at once
699: codex exec "Create a complete REST API with auth, CRUD for users/posts/comments, \
700:   rate limiting, caching, logging, monitoring, tests, and deployment config" \
701:   --model gpt-5.5
702: 
703: # GOOD: Incremental (Pattern 9)
704: codex exec "Create type definitions for a blog API: User, Post, Comment" \
705:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
706: # Then build on top incrementally
707: ```
708: 
709: ### 5. Background Tasks Writing the Same Files
710: 
711: ```bash
712: # BAD: Parallel writes to overlapping files
713: codex exec "Fix auth" --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 &
714: codex exec "Fix auth tests" --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5 &
715: # Race condition: both modify src/auth/ simultaneously
716: 
717: # GOOD: Background only for independent, read-only analysis
718: codex exec "Review src/auth/" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
719:   > /tmp/auth-review.txt &
720: codex exec "Review src/payments/" --sandbox read-only --model gpt-5.5 \
721:   > /tmp/pay-review.txt &
722: wait
723: ```
724: 
725: ### 6. Using --oss for Production Workflows
726: 
727: ```bash
728: # BAD: OSS models in automated pipelines (unpredictable quality)
729: codex exec "Fix the authentication bug" --oss --model gpt-5.5
730: 
731: # GOOD: Use --oss only for local experimentation
732: # For production workflows, always use gpt-5.5 with ChatGPT OAuth (codex login)
733: codex exec "Fix the authentication bug" --model gpt-5.5
734: ```
735: 
736: ### 7. Backgrounding codex exec Inside Shell Scripts Called by Another AI
737: 
738: ```bash
739: # BAD: & inside the shell command - orchestrator sees instant exit 0
740: codex exec "Deep review all phases" --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt 2>&1 &
741: echo "PID: $!"
742: # The Bash tool reports "completed" in <2 seconds. Codex is still running.
743: 
744: # GOOD: No & - use the orchestrator's own background mechanism instead
745: # In Claude Code: Bash(command="codex exec ...", run_in_background=true)
746: # In Copilot: background delegation
747: # The orchestrator waits for the actual codex process to finish.
748: codex exec "Deep review all phases" --full-auto -o /tmp/result.txt 2>&1
749: ```
750: 
751: This is the most common false-completion trap in cross-AI orchestration. The orchestrating AI reads empty output files and either hallucinates results or reports stale data from a prior run.
752: 
753: ### 8. Forgetting Context in Stateless exec Calls
754: 
755: ```bash
756: # BAD: Follow-up without re-providing context
757: codex exec "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model gpt-5.5  # Turn 1
758: codex exec "Now fix the issue you found" --model gpt-5.5  # Turn 2: Codex has no memory of Turn 1
759: 
760: # GOOD: Re-provide context or use session resume
761: codex exec "Analyze src/auth.ts" --model gpt-5.5 > /tmp/analysis.txt
762: codex exec "@src/auth.ts Fix the issues identified: $(cat /tmp/analysis.txt)" \
763:   --sandbox workspace-write --model gpt-5.5
764: ```

18: # cli-codex Providers, Models & Invocation
19: 
20: The single catalog of the provider, model ids, defaults, `model_reasoning_effort` lever, and dispatch shapes the cli-codex mode can reach.
21: 
22: ---
23: 
24: ## 1. OVERVIEW
25: 
26: ### Core Principle
27: One place to answer "which model, which effort, how to dispatch" for cli-codex. This mode is single-provider (OpenAI via ChatGPT OAuth) — the choice space is one provider, five models, and one effort ladder capped per model.
28: 
29: ### When to Use
30: - Choosing a `--model` for a `codex exec` dispatch
31: - Mapping a desired reasoning effort onto `-c model_reasoning_effort=` for a given model (and staying under its ceiling)
32: - Recalling the default model + effort + service tier and the canonical non-interactive invocation shape
33: 
34: ### Scope
35: This file enumerates the provider/model/effort facts and the dispatch envelope. It does NOT own: the full `codex exec` flag surface, sandbox modes, auth pre-flight, or troubleshooting (see [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md)), the cross-AI orchestration patterns (see [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md)), per-model prompt-craft (see §6), or the fan-out / model-enforcement runtime (see §6).
36: 
37: ### Authority pointers
38: - Full CLI flags, subcommands, sandbox modes, auth pre-flight, troubleshooting → [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md)
39: - Dispatch envelope + orchestration patterns + failure-mode traps → [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md)
40: - Default-invocation contract → [../SKILL.md](../SKILL.md)
41: - Routing, intent map, resource map, loading levels and the self-invocation guard → [../ROUTER.md](../ROUTER.md)
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ## 2. PROVIDERS & MODELS
46: 
47: cli-codex is backed by a single provider — **OpenAI**, authenticated through ChatGPT OAuth only (`codex login`; no API key). The model string passed to `--model` / `-m` is a bare OpenAI slug. All five models run on the `fast` service tier (`-c service_tier="fast"`); each caps at a different reasoning-effort ceiling.
48: 
49: ### OpenAI
50: 
51: | Model id | Default? | Effort ceiling / notes |
52: |----------|----------|------------------------|
53: | `gpt-5.5` | **Default** | Ceiling `xhigh`; default effort `medium`. General delegation — generation, review, docs, architecture, research |
54: | `gpt-6-luna` | — | Ceiling `max`. Implementation-heavy work wanting deeper reasoning; the `luna-impl` profile pins `max` |
55: | `gpt-5.6-terra` | — | Ceiling `ultra`. GPT-5.6 fast sibling; no dedicated config profile — call directly via `-m gpt-5.6-terra` |
56: | `gpt-6.1-terra` | — | Ceiling `ultra`. The newest Terra model, which the Codex catalog lists as GPT-6.1 Terra with efforts `low` through `ultra`. No dedicated config profile, so call it directly via `-m gpt-6.1-terra` |
57: | `gpt-6-sol` | — | Ceiling `ultra`. Verification / review and the hardest planning; shares the `ultra` ceiling with Terra; the `sol-verify` profile pins `xhigh` |
58: 
59: `--oss` (local Ollama models) exists as an escape hatch for local experimentation only — not a production dispatch target. See [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md) §4.
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ## 3. DEFAULTS & QUICK INVOCATION
64: 
65: Dispatch this mode's default without opening any other file:
66: 
67: | Field | Value |
68: |-------|-------|
69: | Default model | `gpt-5.5` |
70: | Default effort | `-c model_reasoning_effort="medium"` |
71: | Service tier | `-c service_tier="fast"` |
72: | Default sandbox | `--sandbox workspace-write` (for edits) / `read-only` (for review/analysis) |
73: 
74: ```bash
75: codex exec \
76:   --model gpt-5.5 \
77:   -c model_reasoning_effort="medium" \
78:   -c service_tier="fast" \
79:   -c approval_policy=never \
80:   --sandbox workspace-write \
81:   "<prompt>"
82: ```
83: 
84: Honor explicit user phrasing verbatim ("Use gpt 5.5 high fast", "Use gpt 6 sol ultra"). Model stays on `gpt-5.5` and service tier stays on `fast` unless the user names a different one; keep the effort within the chosen model's ceiling (§4). If Codex is not authenticated, the mode ASKS the user to run `codex login` — it never substitutes an API key or a different model. See the auth pre-flight decision tree in [../SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) §3.
85: 
86: ---
87: 
88: ## 4. REASONING-EFFORT / THINKING LEVER
89: 
90: cli-codex expresses reasoning effort through the config override **`-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"`**. There is **no `--reasoning-effort`, `--reasoning`, or `--quiet` flag** — the config override is the only lever. The `fast` service tier is a separate axis set with `-c service_tier="fast"`.
91: 
92: **Effort ladder** (ascending, 8 levels): `none` · `minimal` · `low` · `medium` · `high` · `xhigh` · `max` · `ultra`.
93: 
94: Per-model ceilings — set the effort within the chosen model's cap:
95: 
96: | Model | Effort ceiling | Notes |
97: |-------|----------------|-------|
98: | `gpt-5.5` | `xhigh` | Default effort `medium` |
99: | `gpt-6-luna` | `max` | `luna-impl` profile pins `max` |
100: | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `ultra` | Callable directly; no dedicated profile |
101: | `gpt-6.1-terra` | `ultra` | Callable directly; no dedicated profile |
102: | `gpt-6-sol` | `ultra` | `sol-verify` profile pins `xhigh` |
103: 
104: Selection heuristic: default `gpt-5.5 medium`; raise to `high` / `xhigh` for architecture, security, and complex planning; escalate the model when the task wants reasoning past `xhigh` — `gpt-6-luna max` for implementation, `gpt-6-sol xhigh` / `ultra` for verification and review; drop to `low` / `minimal` for trivial lookups. Effort can also live in `config.toml`, a `[profiles.<name>]` block, or `plan_mode_reasoning_effort` — see [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md) §5.
105: 
106: ---
107: 
108: ## 5. HOW TO INVOKE
109:

113: ```
114:

116: 
117: ### Dispatch envelope (child / detached sessions)
118: When dispatching as a non-interactive child (spec-gate-neutralized worker), prefix the shared env and terminate stdin:
119: 
120: ```bash
121: SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1 codex exec \
122:   --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high" -c service_tier="fast" \
123:   -c approval_policy=never --sandbox workspace-write \
124:   "<prompt>" </dev/null > stdout.log 2>&1
125: ```
126: 
127: - `SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1` — neutralizes the spec-gate for a bound child worker so it does not stall waiting on an interactive Gate-3 answer, and shares the parent's worktree instead of allocating its own.
128: - `</dev/null` — REQUIRED when backgrounding `codex exec` inside a `while read … done < file` loop; without it the backgrounded process inherits and drains the loop's stdin, silently dropping most dispatches. See [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md) §4 → "Silent Stdin Consumption".
129: 
130: ### Self-invocation guard
131: A codex dispatch must not recursively re-enter a session already running inside Codex (detection: `CODEX_SESSION_ID` / any `CODEX_*` env var, `codex` in process ancestry, or `~/.codex/state/<id>/lock`). The guard refuses the dispatch — see [../ROUTER.md](../ROUTER.md) §3 "Self-Invocation Guard".
132: 
133: ### Parallel / fan-out
134: Multi-lineage parallel dispatch is driven by the shared deep-loop runtime (`fanout-run.cjs`, executor kind `cli-codex`), which lives outside this hub — see §6.
135: 
136: ---
137: 
138: ## 6. ENFORCEMENT & PROFILES (authoritative elsewhere — do not duplicate here)
139: 
140: - **Fan-out dispatcher** → `.skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/scripts/fanout-run.cjs` (executor kind `cli-codex`)
141: - **Named config profiles** (`luna-impl`, `sol-verify`, `review`, `debug`, …) → one `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` file per profile, selected with `-p <name>`; roster and routing in [agent-delegation.md](./agent-delegation.md)
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 7. RELATED
146: 
147: - [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md) — full `codex exec` flags, sandbox modes, model table, auth, config, troubleshooting
148: - [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md) — cross-AI orchestration patterns + dispatch failure-mode traps

14: # Codex CLI Hook Contract
15: 
16: ---
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: Codex CLI 0.130.0 exposes native hooks behind the stable `hooks` feature flag.
21: Spec Kit uses the native `SessionStart` and `UserPromptSubmit` surfaces
22: to inject startup context and the compact skill-advisor brief.
23: 
24: ---
25: 
26: ## 2. ACTIVATION
27: 
28: Hooks are inert unless enabled:
29: 
30: ```toml
31: [features]
32: hooks = true
33: ```
34: 
35: `codex --enable hooks ...` is an equivalent process-local override. The
36: Superset `codex` wrapper already passes this flag, but `~/.codex/config.toml`
37: should still include it so direct Codex invocations behave the same way.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 3. REGISTRATION
42: 
43: Codex reads hook entries from the user-global `~/.codex/hooks.json` and, for a
44: trusted checkout, from the checkout's own `.codex/hooks.json`. Both use the
45: Claude-style outer array plus nested `hooks` array shape:
46: 
47: ```json
48: {
49:   "hooks": {
50:     "SessionStart": [
51:       {
52:         "hooks": [
53:           {
54:             "type": "command",
55:             "command": "node /absolute/path/to/session-start.js",
56:             "timeout": 3
57:           }
58:         ]
59:       }
60:     ],
61:     "UserPromptSubmit": [
62:       {
63:         "hooks": [
64:           {
65:             "type": "command",
66:             "command": "node /absolute/path/to/user-prompt-submit.js",
67:             "timeout": 3
68:           }
69:         ]
70:       }
71:     ]
72:   }
73: }
74: ```
75: 
76: When appending Spec Kit hooks, preserve existing Superset `notify.sh`
77: entries. Multiple hooks for one event run concurrently, so hook commands must be
78: idempotent and must not rely on registration order.
79: 
80: ### 3.1 Tool-Level Guard Adapters (Claude / OpenCode parity)
81: 
82: Beyond the session-lifecycle hooks, Codex mirrors the repo's guard hooks as thin
83: adapters over the same runtime-neutral cores the Claude hooks and OpenCode plugins
84: use. Each fails open (exit 0 on empty/malformed stdin); the two deny-capable guards
85: emit `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny"`, which Codex honors.
86: 
87: | Event · matcher | Guard | Adapter |
88: |---|---|---|
89: | PreToolUse · `exec\|Bash\|apply_patch\|edit` | spec-gate enforce (deny-capable) | `system-spec-kit/runtime/hooks/codex/spec-gate-enforce.mjs` |
90: | UserPromptSubmit | spec-gate classify (state only, no emit) | `system-spec-kit/runtime/hooks/codex/spec-gate-classify.mjs` |
91: | PreToolUse · `exec\|Bash` | dispatch preflight lint (deny-capable) | `.skilled/hooks/dispatch/codex/dispatch-preflight-lint.mjs` |
92: | PostToolUse · `apply_patch\|edit` | post-edit quality | `.skilled/hooks/post-edit-quality/codex/post-edit-quality.cjs` |
93: | PostToolUse · `exec\|Bash` | dispatch audit (observe) | `.skilled/hooks/dispatch/codex/dispatch-audit-posttooluse.mjs` |
94: | Stop | completion-evidence sentinel (advisory) | `system-spec-kit/runtime/hooks/codex/completion-evidence-stop.cjs` |
95: | PreToolUse · `mcp__.*` | mcp route guard (dormant until an external MCP family registers) | `.skilled/hooks/mcp-route-guard/codex/mcp-route-guard.cjs` |
96: 
97: > Codex delivers an `apply_patch` target path inside `tool_input.command` (the
98: > `*** Add/Update/Delete File:` header), not a `file_path` field — filePath-driven
99: > adapters parse the path from the patch body. A Stop hook's stdout is parsed as a
100: > response envelope, so neutral shell scripts wired to Stop must not emit stdout.
101: 
102: > Codex 0.160 renamed its shell tool from `exec` to `Bash`, and a matcher of
103: > `exec` alone no longer fires for a shell call. Every shell matcher names both.
104: > The same release hands PostToolUse the shell output as one string where older
105: > builds handed `{stdout, stderr}`, so the audit adapter reads either shape.
106: 
107: > Codex runs a project hook only after the operator approves that exact entry.
108: > The approval is stored in `~/.codex/config.toml` under `[hooks.state."..."]` as a
109: > `trusted_hash`, and an entry with no approval is skipped without a warning. Because
110: > the approval is a hash, a changed entry is likely to need approving again. After a
111: > `hooks.json` change, open `/hooks` in an interactive Codex session and approve every
112: > entry it lists as needing review.
113: 
114: > Codex has no task-dispatch guard. Its `spawn_agent` call reaches PreToolUse as
115: > `collaborationspawn_agent`, but the hook payload carries the spawn `message`
116: > encrypted (`gAAAAA...`) beside `task_name` and `fork_turns`, so the guard has no
117: > prompt or target to check.
118: 
119: Codex loads the full repo hook set (lifecycle and guards) from `.codex/hooks.json`.
120: The user-global `~/.codex/hooks.json` must hold no copy of it, or every hook runs
121: twice. `.skilled/bin/install-codex-hooks.mjs` removes such copies, backs up first,
122: and keeps Superset and other third-party entries.
123: 
124: ---
125: 
126: ## 4. EVENT INPUTS
127: 
128: Hook commands receive JSON on stdin. Current generated schemas use snake_case
129: field names and reject unknown properties.
130: 
131: `SessionStart` required shape:
132: 
133: ```json
134: {
135:   "session_id": "uuid",
136:   "transcript_path": null,
137:   "cwd": "/workspace",
138:   "hook_event_name": "SessionStart",
139:   "model": "gpt-5.5",
140:   "permission_mode": "default",
141:   "source": "startup"
142: }
143: ```
144: 
145: `source` is `startup`, `resume`, or `clear`.
146: 
147: `UserPromptSubmit` adds turn-scoped prompt fields:
148: 
149: ```json
150: {
151:   "session_id": "uuid",
152:   "turn_id": "uuid",
153:   "transcript_path": null,
154:   "cwd": "/workspace",
155:   "hook_event_name": "UserPromptSubmit",
156:   "model": "gpt-5.5",
157:   "permission_mode": "default",
158:   "prompt": "user prompt"
159: }
160: ```
161: 
162: ---
163: 
164: ## 5. EVENT OUTPUTS
165: 
166: Use JSON output for model-visible context:
167: 
168: ```json
169: {
170:   "hookSpecificOutput": {
171:     "hookEventName": "UserPromptSubmit",
172:     "additionalContext": "Advisor: live; use sk-code 0.91/0.23 pass."
173:   }
174: }
175: ```
176: 
177: For `SessionStart`, set `"hookEventName": "SessionStart"` and put startup
178: context in `additionalContext`.
179: 
180: Codex also accepts plain stdout for context on injecting events, but JSON is the
181: preferred Spec Kit path because it is explicit and testable. Context is recorded
182: as a developer-role message in the conversation state. For `SessionStart`, it is
183: placed before the first user prompt; for `UserPromptSubmit`, it is placed after
184: the submitted user message.
185: 
186: ---
187: 
188: ## 6. EXIT AND TIMEOUT SEMANTICS
189: 
190: | Condition | Behavior |
191: | --- | --- |
192: | Exit `0` | Success. Output is parsed and injected when `additionalContext` is present. |
193: | `UserPromptSubmit` exit `2` with stderr | Blocks the turn; stderr becomes the reason. |
194: | Other non-zero exits | Fail-open. Codex logs the hook failure and continues the turn. |
195: | Timeout | Fail-open. Default is 600 seconds unless `timeout` / `timeoutSec` is set. |
196: 
197: Spec Kit hooks use short per-hook timeouts in registration and return `{}` on
198: fail-open paths. The prompt hook emits a bounded stale advisory on cold-start
199: timeout so the user can see the advisor surface is installed.
200: 
201: ---
202: 
203: ## 7. SPEC KIT HOOK WIRING
204: 
205: Installed paths:
206: 
207: - `SessionStart`: `.skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/dist/hooks/codex/session-start.js`
208: - `UserPromptSubmit`: `.skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/dist/hooks/codex/user-prompt-submit.js`
209: 
210: Manual smoke checks:
211: 
212: ```bash
213: printf '%s\n' '{"session_id":"s1","hook_event_name":"SessionStart","source":"startup","cwd":"'"$PWD"'","model":"gpt-5.5","permission_mode":"default"}' \
214:   | node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/dist/hooks/codex/session-start.js
215: ```
216: 
217: ```bash
218: printf '%s\n' '{"prompt":"implement TypeScript hook","cwd":"'"$PWD"'"}' \
219:   | node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/dist/hooks/codex/user-prompt-submit.js
220: ```
221: 
222: Expected stdout is `{}` or a JSON object with
223: `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext`; for matching work prompts it should be
224: non-empty and start with `Advisor:` on the prompt hook.
225: 
226: ---
227: 
228: ## 8. SOURCES
229: 
230: - OpenAI Codex source schema:
231:   `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/codex/main/codex-rs/hooks/src/schema.rs`
232: - OpenAI Codex issue evidence for five native events and the original experimental `codex_hooks` flag:
233:   `https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/16226`
234: - OpenAI Codex issue evidence for `UserPromptSubmit.additionalContext` becoming
235:   model-visible developer context:
236:   `https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/16933`
237: - Packet-local synthesis:
238:   `<spec-folder>`
